name: memoizing-parser
intent: Turn a backtracking recursive-descent parser into a linear-time one by memoizing every rule result - success and failure alike - under a key of rule and input position, so that no rule is ever evaluated twice at the same position.
problem: A backtracking parser (recursive descent, PEG, parser combinators) re-tries the same rule at the same input position over and over: ordered choice, longest-match rules and lookahead predicates all send the parser back to positions it has already parsed, and the number of re-evaluations can grow exponentially with the input, so a grammar that is convenient to write has an unpredictable cost. The decision is whether to buy a linear worst case by storing every intermediate rule/position result, and how to key that store - a bare position is only sound while the rules are stateless.
context: Applies to hand-written or combinator-based parsers whose grammar is expressed as mutually recursive rules over a position or token index - PEGs, scannerless parsers, DSL front ends, language tooling - where unlimited lookahead or heavy ordered-choice backtracking is wanted without rewriting the grammar into LL(k)/LR form. It presupposes that the whole input is available up front (or at least that the position space is stable), that memory proportional to the input length is acceptable, and that the memoized rules are pure functions of the input position, or can be keyed with whatever state they read.
benefits: Guarantees linear parse time while keeping full backtracking and unlimited lookahead: each rule/position pair is evaluated at most once, so the exponential blow-up of ordered choice and lookahead predicates disappears.
Caching failures is what makes the guarantee hold - the pathological case is not a rule that succeeds repeatedly but one that fails deep into the input and is retried from every alternative.
The transformation is local and mechanical: route each rule through one memo lookup/store pair keyed by position; the grammar, the rule bodies and the semantic actions stay as they were.

Grammar composition gets easier: because a decision may consult the complete result of any nonterminal rather than k terminals of lookahead, ordered choice, longest-match, followed-by/not-followed-by predicates and integrated lexical analysis become cheap to express.

Rules degenerate into pure functions of position, which makes them testable in isolation (call one rule at one offset) and makes the memo table itself a queryable record of every attempted rule/position pair for diagnostics and tooling.

Predictable worst case for input that the application does not control: untrusted or machine-generated text cannot push the parser into super-linear time, so parse cost stays a linear function of input length.
tradeoffs: Memory grows with the input, not with nesting depth: the memo holds an entry for every rule/position pair that was attempted (Ford measured 301-695 bytes of live heap per input byte for a Java parser), and the algorithm needs the whole input, so streaming or line-by-line REPL parsing is out of scope.

Every rule entry pays a lookup and, on a miss, a store, even where no backtracking occurs - Peggy's --cache option documents exactly this trade (no more pathological exponential time, slower parser), so on an already predictive grammar the table is pure overhead.

The position-only key silently assumes stateless rules: layout/indentation sensitivity, a type-name table built while declarations are parsed (C/C++), symbol tables or state-reading semantic predicates all produce stale results unless the key carries that state or the table is reset at each state change.

One result per rule/position can be memoized, so the grammar must be locally unambiguous (ordered choice or an explicit tie-break inside the rule); grammars that expect global ambiguity resolution cannot use it.

Left recursion must be rewritten into a right-recursive form or handled by seed growing (as the Scala library does, following Warth/Douglass/Millstein), otherwise the rule's lookup during its own evaluation is circular.

The memo is per-parse state: sharing it across inputs, grammar configurations or parser instances yields wrong parses that still look fast and deterministic, so table ownership and clearing are part of the pattern, not an afterthought.

participants.responsibility: One grammar production expressed as a function or method of the input position; it opens with a memo lookup and closes with a memo store, but its body remains ordinary backtracking recursive descent.
Per-parse table indexed by (rule, position) - dense per-rule columns or a hash map on a packed key - holding one entry per attempted pair; it is the only state the pattern adds.

The stored outcome of one rule at one position: a success (semantic value plus the position after the match) or a recorded failure; 'not yet computed' must be distinguishable from 'computed and failed'.
The cursor that rule calls recurse over (byte, character or token offset); positions are bounded by the input length, which is what makes a dense table possible.
Ordered choice, repetition, longest-match and lookahead predicates that re-enter rules at positions already tried; it is the source of the redundant calls the memo absorbs.
Optional companion that records the leftmost-furthest failure for error messages, because the first failure stored at a position is not the informative one.

use_cases: PEG and scannerless parsers for programming languages or DSLs whose grammar uses ordered choice with deep alternatives and integrated lexical analysis.
Hand-written recursive-descent parsers that need unlimited lookahead (longest-match, followed-by/not-followed-by predicates) without being rewritten into LL(k)/LR shape.

Parser-combinator front ends whose rules are authored separately and composed, so a rule's result must be reusable however often the composition re-enters it - the reason the Scala library ships PackratParsers.
Interactive language tooling that parses the same input repeatedly at the same offsets (editors, REPL completion, incremental analysis), where per-position results can be reused across passes.

Front ends for grammars that cannot be disambiguated with bounded lookahead (nested generics/array syntax, expressions with ambiguous prefixes) yet must still run in worst-case linear time on untrusted input.
Peggy-generated JavaScript or TypeScript parsers with the cache option enabled when pathological backtracking must be bounded, accepting the documented overhead on ordinary inputs.
Scala parser-combinator grammars that mix in PackratParsers, using PackratReader memoization for unlimited lookahead and left-recursive productions.
Racket's packrat parsing library for parser combinators that need PEG-style backtracking without recomputing rule results at the same input position.
avoid_when: The grammar is (or can cheaply be made) LL(1)/predictive: a plain recursive-descent parser uses memory proportional to nesting depth and no table at all, and a cache would only add lookup cost.
Inputs are large and flat - machine-generated JSON/CSV/XML-style data - where backtracking is minimal and an input-sized memo is pure overhead (Ford's own example of what not to parse this way).
The parser must work incrementally on a stream or line by line (interactive REPL, network input): the algorithm wants the whole input and a stable position space.

The rules are stateful by design (indentation-sensitive layout, type-name tables, symbol-table lookups): either move those rules out of the memoized set or extend the key with the state, otherwise the cache answers with stale results.
Memory is the binding constraint (embedded targets, small heaps, very large inputs): the memo's constant factor is measured in hundreds of bytes per input byte.
anti_patterns: Memoizing stateful rules under a (rule, position) key without extending the key or resetting the table: the parser stays fast and deterministic while returning parses that belong to an earlier state.

Caching successes but recomputing failures (or treating a missing entry as failure): the exponential worst case is exactly the repeated failing alternative, so the guarantee is lost while the memory cost is still paid.
One global memo table reused across inputs, grammar configurations or parser instances, producing cross-input contamination that stays invisible until the input changes.
Switching memoization on for every parser 'for speed' - on a predictive grammar the table is pure overhead (Peggy documents --cache as making the parser slower).
Reading the error report out of the memo: the first failure recorded at a position is not the furthest one, so leftmost-furthest reporting has to be tracked separately.
design_principles: Memoize pure functions: the key must capture everything a rule's result depends on - rule identity plus position, plus parser state wherever a rule reads it.
Cache failures as first-class results, never as absent entries.
Separate mechanism from grammar: the rules stay ordinary functions; the lookup/store pair is applied uniformly at rule entry.
Own the table's lifecycle: one table per parse, sized from the input length and discarded with it.
Preserve the guarantee: any combinator or loop that evaluates rule bodies without passing through the memo wrapper (hidden recursion) reintroduces super-linear time.
best_practices: Route every rule through a single memo helper so that key construction and hit/miss logic exist once.

Represent 'not computed' and 'computed and failed' distinctly (three-state enum, nested optional, or an explicit sentinel where the map cannot store null - Java's ConcurrentHashMap, Kotlin's getOrPut).
Key on (rule id, position) with positions bounded by the input length (n+1 columns per rule) and pre-size the table from the input instead of growing it during the parse.

Copy the memo entry out before recursing when the language holds references into the table (Rust's borrow checker), or split the table per rule so recursion never needs a second mutable borrow of the same structure.
Scope and clear the table per parse; never share it across inputs, threads (Go maps, C# Dictionary and Java HashMap are not safe for concurrent use) or grammar configurations.
Keep stateful rules out of the memoized set, or fold their state into the key, and mix memoized with non-memoized rules explicitly - the Scala library documents that option.
Track leftmost-furthest failure separately from the memo so error messages stay informative.
sources: Parr, Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010) - Pattern 6, Memoizing Parser (ch. 3, Enhanced Parsing Patterns, p. 80), following pattern 5 Backtracking Parser: memoize a rule's result at an input position so backtracking stays linear.

Ford, Packrat Parsing: Simple, Powerful, Lazy, Linear Time (ICFP 2002) - the result matrix with one row per nonterminal and one column per input position, cached failures, linear time with unlimited lookahead, and the determinism/statelessness/space limitations.
Warth, Douglass & Millstein, Packrat Parsers Can Support Left Recursion (PEPM 2008) - seed-growing algorithm cited by the Scala parser-combinators implementation for its left-recursive rules.
